newsitem.title: USA: FEATURE - Getting objective about your investments.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE - Getting objective about your investments.

text.p: How did your investments do last year? Did you beat the market? Did you meet the market? Did you do as well as could be expected given the types of investments you have?
Could you have done better with your money under the mattress or in a plain vanilla stock index fund?
These are the kinds of measures that professional money managers call "benchmarking" and they are crucial to long term investment success.

If you really want to know how you are doing, you have to compare your investment performance with some alternatives. The best time to do that is now, when you can analyse last year's performance and plan this year's goals.

"The benchmark is the bottom line of the most important part of the investment process," when goals for performance and risk are determined, says Andrew Mehalko, research director of DCA Global Investment Management in Fort Lauderdale.

Mehalko and David Cook, the firm's president, meet annually with their money management clients to determine their client's investment goals for the year and pick an appropriate benchmark against which to manage their performance.

They assess each client's need to earn money and ability to tolerate investment risk. Then they develop a mix that is conservative, moderate or aggressive for each client. Then they tie that mix to the market.
For example, one client might be termed "moderate," an outlook that DCA would match with a portfolio of 25 percent U.S. stocks, 25 percent international stocks, and 50 percent long term bonds.

Cook and Mehalko would set a benchmark for this client's portfolio of which 25 percent was the Standard and Poor's 500 stock index, 25 percent the Morgan Stanley international equity index (EAFE, for Europe, Austral-Asia, Far East), and 50 percent for the Lehman Brother's government/corporate long term bond index.
Does this mean that Cook and Mehalko are investing in those indexes? No, they are aiming to beat or match those indexes with their own methods of investment.

At the end of the year, the firm sends clients a year end statement comparing their after-expense results with the benchmark they set at the beginning of the year. They compare performance, but also risk, which investment professionals can quantify through measures of volatility and deviation.

Tom Bellhy, president of Fort Pitt Capital Group in Pittsburgh, takes a more detailed approach to benchmarking. He presents his clients with a raft of indexes so they can compare each piece of their portfolio with an industry average. There's a separate index for small stocks and big stocks, for government long term bonds and international bonds and emerging stocks and convertible securities.

"You could just buy a Lehman brothers index fund and a Vanguard stock index fund and not bother to hire a manager" he recognises. "You use an investment manager to deliver added value" in the form of less risk than the aggressive indexes and more return than the safe ones. If you are using an investment manager, he or she should be willing to compare the volatility, risk and returns he produces for you with a comparable index after fees are deducted.
What if you are your own investment manager? Here are some guidelines for how to set a benchmark for your own investment returns, garnered from the experience of Bellhy and Cook.

-- Avoid setting more than one benchmark goal for the same investment: For example, a better return than the S&P 500, safer than Treasury bills, more buying power than the Consumer Price Index. That's not very realistic and not very helpful.

-- Compare your investments to the indexes they match. If you want to monitor a big stock fund, use the S&P 500. If you are investing in funds that buy small cap stocks, either use an index of small cap stock funds, tracked by both Lipper Analytical in New York and Morningstar in Chicago, or the Standard & Poor's 600 small stock index. Don't bother to compare your investments to the Dow Jones industrial average, unless you have a portfolio made up of big industrial stocks.

-- Just for fun, set a benchmark for your own investments against that of a "no brainer" portfolio. What if you assembled a portfolio of really cheap stock index and bond funds and then ignored it forever? How would this investment do, net of fees and transaction costs and on an after -axe basis, compared with your own investment efforts. If you're not beating the mix, the management fees and transaction costs you are covering may not be worth it.

-- Remember that the way you time investments can affect your benchmarking. Try to track the indexes as if you were buying and selling them at the same time as you are your investments. If you get these comparisons from your advisor, make sure they are time weighted to clear out the statistical problems that can be caused by differences in buying times.

-- Next year, be honest. If you or your advisor are failing to beat generic benchmarks either through safer performance or better performance, look to change your approach. Pension fund managers, among the most sophisticated investors of all, have been doing this for years.
